title: Al-Qayyum, the Self-Subsisting
tomorrow: "did He not find thee...?" find you how, exactly?

cards: Somewhere tonight a nurse, a power-plant tech and an air traffic controller are on the night shift. They stay awake so a whole city can sleep, and nobody downtown knows their names. Ayat al-Kursi has that shape.
Right after the Alive comes today's Name, Al-Qayyum, and then the line from yesterday: neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him. Someone is always on shift. That's the answer.
Because He doesn't sleep, we can.

teach.h: STANDS BY HIMSELF, HOLDS ALL ELSE UP.
teach.b: Pickthall renders Al-Qayyum as the Eternal, but the word reaches further: the one who stands by Himself, needing nothing, and holds everything else up.

teach.h: HE GRASPETH THE HEAVENS AND THE EARTH.
teach.b: Surah Fatir puts it in a picture: "Lo! Allah graspeth the heavens and the earth that they deviate not." Nothing in creation stands on its own.
Not the sky, not the ground, not the person who has been holding a family together all week.
There's a reason Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime: a hadith says that whoever recites it on going to bed has a guardian from Allah through the night.
And there's a du'a the Prophet, peace be upon him, taught, built on these two Names: Ya Hayyu ya Qayyum, O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek help.

teach.h: NOT LEFT TO MYSELF, NOT FOR A BLINK.
teach.b: In one version it goes on: set right all my affairs, and don't leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight. That prayer doesn't ask to be made stronger.
It asks not to be left alone with only yourself to lean on.
Leaning isn't the failure. Leaning is what creatures are built to do.

how: Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi, with its 'al-Hayy al-Qayyum', before sleep, and call on Allah with 'Ya Hayyu ya Qayyum, bi-rahmatika astaghith' when they need help.

o: the Eternal, who simply lasts the longest
the Upright, who never bends the rules
the Self-Subsisting, who holds all things up

games.q: who holds it up — tap the pairs.
p: stands by Himself, holds all else up
graspeth the heavens and the earth
by Your mercy I seek help

s: Al-Qayyum just means God lasts a very long time
it's the one who needs nothing and holds everything else up: He graspeth the heavens and the earth.
a hadith links reciting Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime with a guardian through the night
a guardian from Allah stays with the one who recites it until morning.

games.q: your project partner insists on doing every part alone, all night, so it's 'right.' she's falling apart and won't say so. what does today's du'a suggest?
o: let her; carrying it alone is her choice to make.
offer to split it; even the du'a asks not to be left to oneself.
tell the teacher she isn't sharing the work fairly.
games.why: Ya Hayyu ya Qayyum asks, in one version, not to be left to yourself for the blink of an eye. only One holds everything up without sleep; the rest of us lean.

practice: Sit back so a wall or the back of your chair takes your full weight. Let your shoulders drop, then your arms, then your jaw, until you're not holding yourself up at all.
For the two minutes, notice how much was being carried for you the whole time.

wordCard.voice: Al-Qayyum. The Self-Subsisting: needing nothing, holding up everything, awake while the city sleeps.

orig.note: Arabic: the Self-Subsisting, who holds everything up; Pickthall's 'the Eternal' in Ayat al-Kursi.

carryVoice: Something to lean on: he holds it up, the sky, the night, and whoever is holding everything else. Sleep well tonight.

sources.q: Lo! Allah graspeth the heavens and the earth that they deviate not

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:255 (al-Hayy al-Qayyum; neither slumber nor sleep)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2311 (Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime: a guardian from Allah through the night)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3524 (Ya Hayyu ya Qayyum, bi-rahmatika astaghith); the fuller du'a ('do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye') in an-Nasa'i's 'Amal al-Yawm wa al-Laylah and al-Hakim
